About 2,145 trees expected to be felled

The current project is a joint venture between "China State Construction Hong Kong", "Aitken Tang", and "China State Construction Civil Engineering". According to a 2024 Legislative Council document, there are approximately 2,270 trees within the project scope, with about 2,145 expected to be felled, including 10 "trees of special value" — Aquilaria sinensis (土沉香) and 2 Ormosia pachycarpa (茸莢紅豆). The authorities plan to replant about 2,140 trees after completion, including Koelreuteria bipinnata (複羽葉欒樹), Magnolia grandiflora (荷花玉蘭), and Michelia champaca (黃蘭), among others.

No shade from large trees — residents say the heat feels even more intense

Reporters recently inspected the area from Marina Cove (匡湖居) to Sai Kung Town Centre and found that trees had been removed along roads in Pak Wai, Marina Cove, Hiram's Highway (白沙灣), Pak Kong, and the section leading to Sai Kung Town Centre. The felling was particularly noticeable around Pak Kong — due to site formation works, reporters visually estimated that nearly one-third of the trees on the hillside had been cut down. Along the road at Tai Chung Hau Village, at least 15 trees in a row had been felled. Some village residents said that with the roadside greenery diminishing, hot weather feels even more oppressive.

Site formation works are under way on the Pak Kong hillside, where trees have been felled.

A hole has been dug into one of the felled large trees, with a bottle of orange juice placed inside.

Unavoidable removal of about 1,900 trees

In response to queries from Dimsum Daily (《集誌社》), the Highways Department said that because the relevant works run very close to vegetation-covered slopes on both sides of the road, some of the trees — mainly those rooted on the slopes — need to be removed or transplanted to free up sufficient space for construction. After investigation, the unavoidable removal of about 1,900 trees remains necessary.

13 Aquilaria sinensis — 11 expected to be felled

The authorities said there are 13 Aquilaria sinensis trees within the project scope. Of these, 11 were assessed as unsuitable for transplanting — based on their form, structure, and growing location — and will be removed; the remaining 2 will be preserved in situ. In addition, one Ormosia pachycarpa, after assessment, was also deemed unsuitable for transplanting and will be removed; one camphor tree originally slated for transplanting was later assessed as needing removal. Three Indian rubber trees (Ficus elastica, 印度榕) will be preserved in situ.

The authorities said the project team will plant about 2,000 trees at suitable locations within the Sai Kung District, such as roadside greening belts, to enhance the landscape along the route and the Sai Kung community environment.

Aquilaria sinensis is a vulnerable species

Aquilaria sinensis is a native Hong Kong tree species, mainly distributed in Sai Kung, the northeastern New Territories, and on Lantau Island. As of 2021, there were approximately 5,000 mature Aquilaria sinensis trees across the territory. The species is classified as rare and is listed as a protected plant under the Protection of Endangered Species of Animals and Plants Ordinance, as well as being rated Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. Because its resin can be refined into the precious fragrance "agarwood" (沉香), mainland "tree-felling gangs" (斬樹黨) once came to Hong Kong — particularly to Sai Kung — to fell the trees illegally in earlier years, with black-market prices exceeding HK$10,000.

As for Ormosia pachycarpa, it is an evergreen tree of the legume family Fabaceae, genus Ormosia, and is listed as a rare and precious plant by the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD). The species was first discovered in Happy Valley in 1850 and is now classified as endangered within China.

Pak Wai Village resident Regina bought a village house some years ago. A self-described "plant fanatic," she decided to buy the house entirely because of an old tree in front of it, which she likened to a "treasure from antiquity." Upon hearing about the tree-felling in the neighbourhood, she said excitedly: "It's 2,000 trees, not 200!" She believes Sai Kung has long enjoyed the reputation of being Hong Kong's "back garden" and questioned, "Without 2,000 trees, can Sai Kung still be called Hong Kong's back garden?"

Self-described "plant fanatic" Regina decided to buy her house in Sai Kung entirely because of an old tree in front of it, which she likened to finding a "treasure from antiquity." (Photo provided by Regina)

She said that trees are living things — some have grown for over a hundred years; once lost, they cannot easily be restored, including the precious Aquilaria sinensis. Taking Pak Wai Village as an example, she said tourists may not remember the village's name but do remember the old tree at the village entrance, which has even become a bus stop landmark. "The reason I can see the mountain is because of these trees. Try having no trees — how am I supposed to see the mountain?" She believes the government should not take a one-size-fits-all approach at the expense of nature conservation.

Residents are deeply attached to the old trees

Another Sai Kung resident, Amy, said three generations of her family, including her children, grew up in Sai Kung. "Seeing the trees gone is like seeing years of growing up gone too." Without wearing glasses, she laughed that over the years she had enjoyed such good eyesight precisely because she was surrounded by greenery — gazing out at a forest of green. "Suddenly they cut the trees down, and the children are going to end up nearsighted."

Beyond witnessing the disappearance of the trees, she lamented the changes she has seen in Sai Kung over the years — for example, the historically significant buildings across from Hiram's Highway, including the 1946-established paint factory "China Paint" (中華製漆) — known for its "Chrysanthemum," "Giraffe," and "Toy" paint brands — is to be demolished and redeveloped into housing. She also gave the example of a recent super typhoon that brought down an old tree in town, which attracted residents to take photos, also reflecting their affection for old trees.

The roadside scenery has become "patchy and unsightly"

Sai Kung resident Mr Tam said that although he does not know the exact number of trees felled, it is obvious the roadside trees are dwindling. "There used to be so many trees, it was comfortable. Now you see it all patchy and messy — it doesn't feel good." He said that when he moved to Sai Kung one or two years ago, large-scale tree felling had not yet begun; he also felt it was a pity that the Aquilaria sinensis were being cut down. He also questioned whether widening the road would help ease congestion, pointing out that going into Sai Kung on holidays is "expected to be jammed up."

An 84-year-old Sai Kung resident, "Uncle" (阿伯), has lived in the area for more than 20 years. He said that since over a thousand trees were felled, the Sai Kung landscape has become unrecognisable, and he questioned, "What does traffic congestion have to do with the trees? Cars don't drive through the trees, do they?"

Friends of the Earth (地球之友) director Wong Cheuk-yuet (王卓粵) said that when project consultants assess trees, although not necessarily intentional, for the convenience of construction it is easy to end up "nitpicking" — "if it can't be moved, then cut it down" — rather than trying to save each tree tree by tree. For example, ordinary species must be almost "perfect" to be kept; some trees, even if in reasonable condition, are listed with negative factors if they have minor defects or slightly less growing space. For large trees, transplanting can easily cost over a million dollars, or the tree may deteriorate during the process or while searching for a suitable location.

Aquilaria sinensis should in principle be preserved as far as possible

He acknowledged that some locations in Sai Kung are on slopes, where digging out root balls and transplanting are more difficult, but if conservation is the goal, major crown pruning and reducing the size of the root ball should be considered, with "preserving the species" and "saving its life" as the top priorities. With the number of Aquilaria sinensis in sharp decline, the trees should in principle be preserved as far as possible. He is also concerned that as the road gains additional lanes and dividing facilities, there will be less space for planting along the route, transforming what was once a tree-shaded path into a large expanse of concrete, which in the long run may affect the experience of waiting for buses and walking along the road.
